faqs.a: Both measure the same profit, but margin divides by selling price while markup divides by cost. A $40 profit on a $100 sale is 40% margin and 66.7% markup.
faqs.q: What is the difference between margin and markup?

faqs.a: No. Margin = profit / price, and profit can never exceed price (cost would have to be negative). If you need more than 100%, you are thinking of markup, which has no ceiling.
Use the cost + margin mode: enter your cost and 40. The calculator returns price = cost / 0.60. A $60 cost needs a $100 price for 40% margin.
faqs.q: How do I price for a 40% margin?

faqs.a: Retail and most services quote margin (share of the selling price). Manufacturing and contracting often use markup on cost. Pick the one your industry speaks, and convert when comparing.
faqs.q: Which should I use for my business?

faqs.a: Gross - it uses direct cost only. Net margin subtracts rent, salaries, taxes, and everything else, and needs your full profit-and-loss statement.
faqs.q: Is this gross or net margin?

faqs.a: No. Everything is computed in your browser.

margin-markup-calculator.formula:
Profit = price - cost
Margin % = profit / price x 100
Markup % = profit / cost x 100
From margin: price = cost / (1 - margin/100)
From markup: cost = price / (1 + markup/100)

keyFacts: Margin = profit / selling price x 100. Markup = profit / cost x 100.
The same $40 profit is a 40% margin but a 66.7% markup - the denominator changes everything.
Margin can never reach 100% (that would need zero cost); markup has no upper limit.
Retailers usually think in margin; wholesalers and contractors often quote markup.
To convert: price = cost / (1 - margin); cost = price / (1 + markup).
Mixing the two up is the most common pricing mistake in small business.

margin-markup-calculator.workedExample:
Cost $60, selling price $100:
1. Profit = 100 - 60 = $40
2. Margin = 40 / 100 x 100 = 40%
3. Markup = 40 / 60 x 100 = 66.67%
Reverse check: cost $60 with 40% margin -> price = 60 / (1 - 0.40) = $100. Matches.
